extracted.intended_audience: British citizens, clergy, and policymakers concerned with the constitution and the spread of revolutionary ideas (late-18th-century educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: A conservative political essay arguing how Britain should preserve its constitution, social order, and religion against revolutionary doctrines and secret societies. It gives normative claims about institutions, eligibility for public office, the role of clergy, and social mores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage secret assemblies and revolutionary conversations
rubrics_metrics.description: We should discourage all secret assemblies, which afford opportunities to the disaffected, and all conversations which foster any notions of political perfection, and create hankerings after unattainable happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such gatherings increase discontents among the unfortunate, the idle, and the worthless, and are fertile ground for conspirators (e.g., Jacobin clubs). Preventing them is presented as a means to preserve liberty and public order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check immorality and licentiousness in every shape
rubrics_metrics.description: Above all, we should be careful to discourage and check immorality and licentiousness in every shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immorality will of itself subvert every government and subject the nation to the tyranny of a profligate mob; therefore moral regulation is a fundamental safeguard of the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public instructors must promote Religion and Virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Public instructors of the nation (clergy) are especially bound to exert themselves in the cause of Religion and Virtue at a time of threat from revolutionary doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Backwardness or indifference by moral instructors will be interpreted as defeat and insincerity; active, earnest, and judicious addresses to the public's moral sentiments are urged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy should be educated in natural philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Our ancestors enacted that the clergy shall be well instructed in natural philosophy, judging that knowledge of the symmetry of nature would produce belief in wisdom and power beyond the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training clergy in natural philosophy helps them use the order and beauty of nature to promote religious conviction and social morals; this is a practical recommendation for clerical education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion and virtue are mutually reinforcing and must be defended
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion and Virtue are considered closely united and mutually supporting each other; corrupters labour to prove this a mistake and aim to explode both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizing their connection is key: moral and religious instruction should be used to counteract propagandists and corrupting influences aiming to undermine social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid political discussion in moral/religious addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Dwelling on moral and religious topics leaves no occasion for political discussion, which would be equally improper and hurtful; such discussions never fail to produce ill-humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While instructors should promote religion and virtue, they should refrain from partisan political debate in those contexts to avoid stirring discord.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit claims of different ranks candidly to preserve peace
rubrics_metrics.description: No where else in Europe are the claims of the different ranks in society so generally and so candidly admitted; this candid admission contributes to peace and constitutional excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A constitution that recognizes and candidly admits the legitimate claims of different social ranks reduces causes of contention and promotes social harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper chamber should function as hereditary magistrates/counsellors, not as class representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Lords is not a representation of a privileged 'order' but a body of hereditary magistrates who sit as the King's counsellors or as judges, not to defend a noble class's privileges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An upper house that acts primarily as a judicial/counsel body mitigates factionalism arising from corporate class interests; it should not be a corporate 'body' defending its own class privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower chamber should represent the whole nation, not a single order
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Commons are the proper representatives of the whole nation and consist of persons of every class—highest birth, great fortune, education, knowledge, and talents—not merely the 'third estate'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation that mixes individuals from various classes removes causes of dissension tied to distinct corporate orders and better serves deliberation for the general good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude the needy and laborious from legislative eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Those whose habits of needy and laborious life have precluded opportunities of acquiring general views of political relations should be excluded from eligibility; such persons are unfit for deliberations where comprehensive views are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: lack of broad education/experience makes such representatives liable to change opinions easily and be duped by demagogues; thus eligibility should be limited to ensure stable, informed deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer land proprietors/gentry as legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all classes, land proprietors (the gentry) are the fittest for holding the important office of representative because of their habits of thinking, general acquaintance with national concerns, and roles settling local differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gentry's recurring public roles (justices of the peace, local arbitration) give them appropriate national perspective and temperate habits for legislative duties; family pride and established manners are useful civic supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of merchant/commercial representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not recommend filling the House of Commons with merchants: the man of purely commercial notions disclaims generosity and values everything by exchange, making him less fit for public deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial mentality prizes monetary valuation and can be venal; history shows gentry were not the most venal part of the House—policy should guard against multiplying venal members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make legislative office costly and restrict suffrage to limit corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: A wise and free legislation will endeavour to make election to office expensive and troublesome, and therefore will neither admit universal suffrage nor very extensive eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting the franchise and eligibility reduces opportunities for corruption and venality, which are seen as principal threats to the aims of civil constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harness and regulate propensities like family pride
rubrics_metrics.description: Propensities such as family pride are not to be rejected; they should be regulated and made use of as means of carrying on national business because they incite propriety, honesty, and useful manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than suppressing natural social propensities, institutions should channel them into public-spirited behavior; their abuse, not their existence, is the problem.
